common_name: Manor Buckwheat (Large-Seeded Canadian Cover Crop Buckwheat)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill into warm soil after all frost danger has passed, since Manor is killed by the lightest freeze.

directions: Manor was released by Agriculture Canada in the 1970s and became the dominant large-seeded buckwheat grown across the Northeast and Canadian prairies through the 1990s, prized for the bold seed size millers want for whole groats and soba flour. Drill or broadcast into a warm, well-worked seedbed once soil has warmed in late spring, then roll or shallow-harrow to firm the seedbed for even emergence. Its rapid, dense canopy smothers summer weeds within a few weeks and can be mowed or turned under at first bloom to build organic matter ahead of a fall crop. Because it carries no frost tolerance, time fall plow-down before the first killing freeze to avoid losing the stand outright.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

common_name: Winsor Royal Buckwheat (Large-Seeded Cover Crop Buckwheat)

planting.note: Sow after soil has warmed and frost risk has passed; this diploid large-seeded type establishes and canopies quickly in warm conditions.

directions: Winsor Royal is a large-seeded diploid buckwheat released by the Winsor Grain Company of Minneapolis in 1982 and grown for its bold, market-acceptable seed alongside a lower test weight than modern hybrid types. Broadcast or drill shallowly into a warm, firm seedbed after frost danger has ended, since seedlings emerge within days but are easily killed by cold soil or frost. The crop forms a dense, fast-closing canopy that shades out weeds and provides a strong nectar source for pollinators through its extended bloom period. Mow or disk under at early flowering for a quick-building green manure, or let a later planting stand into fall as a short-season smother crop ahead of a cover crop rotation.

common_name: Defender Radish (European Oilseed Radish Cover Crop)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill in late summer, roughly 6-10 weeks before the first fall frost, so plants build root mass before winter kill.

directions: Defender is a European-bred oilseed radish selected for a stubbier, more branched taproot than daikon-type tillage radishes, giving it somewhat greater winter hardiness and a lower seed cost per acre. Drill or broadcast in late summer so plants can establish a fibrous root mass and full rosette before the first hard freeze, since it scavenges leftover nitrogen deep in the soil profile and holds it against fall and winter leaching. The dense, branching root system builds channels for water infiltration without the single deep taproot look of Groundhog- or Nitro-type radishes. Foliage and roots winterkill in most temperate zones, leaving a mellow, easily worked residue for spring planting.

planting.note: Direct-sow from spring through midsummer for late-season grazing or cover, since Maris Kestrel is a short, leafy type bred for a long growing window.

directions: Maris Kestrel is a short-stemmed, high leaf-to-stem forage kale bred for excellent digestibility and cold tolerance, widely used to extend the grazing season into winter and as a wildlife food plot planting. Broadcast or drill into a firm, fertile seedbed from spring into midsummer, since the crop needs a long window before it reaches grazing readiness in late fall or winter. Its compact stature and lodging-resistant stems keep leaves off the ground and palatable even after hard frosts sweeten the foliage. Where used strictly as a cover crop, mow or graze off before bolting the following spring to prevent volunteer reseeding.

common_name: Thousand Head Kale (Heirloom English Forage Kale)

planting.note: Direct-sow in late spring to early summer so plants size up into a heavily branched stand before hard frost.

directions: Thousand Head is a traditional English heirloom forage kale, named for its unusually heavy branching habit that produces far more leafy growth points than typical kale types. Sow directly into fertile, well-drained soil in late spring to early summer, thinning or spacing plants to allow the many side branches room to develop. The crop is exceptionally winter hardy, standing through hard frosts and continuing to supply green forage and cover into deep winter when little else survives. Grazed, cut, or left standing as green cover, the dense branching canopy also provides valuable ground cover for wildlife through the cold months.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach
